extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers; writers, artists, and thinkers interested in character, society, and aesthetic philosophy
extracted.subtask_short: essayist guidance on character and art
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical and aesthetic prescriptions about individual character, the nature of genius, and principles of art and society that guide how one should create, judge, and live with artistic and moral integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion in art (unity of whole and detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art, in the artist, is proportion, or a habitual respect to the whole by an eye loving beauty in details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details must be means and never ends; the eye must not lose sight for a moment of the purpose. The artist should avoid working 'here and there and at all points, adding and adding, instead of unfolding the unit of his thought.' Beautiful particulars are necessary, but must serve the overall design; otherwise the work becomes mere jingles. Respect the argument and the unity of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mannerism and tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature abhors mannerism; there is a perpetual tendency to a set mode, a trick which may be soon learned and continued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of falling into a recognizable stylistic trick or habitual manner. Cultivate freshness and resist the ease of repeating a successful stroke. Mannerism diminishes the integrity of art and thought; do not let style substitute for substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value total powers over isolated talents
rubrics_metrics.description: As we grow older we value total powers and effects, as the impression, the quality, the spirit of men and things, rather than solitary excellences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise the habit, the system, the continuous character rather than isolated feats or flattering moments. In judging persons or art, look for sustained unity and habitual force, not merely standout acts that depart from an individual's faith or practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not idealize individuals; expect imperfection
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no such men as we fable; no Jesus, nor Pericles, nor Caesar, nor Angelo, nor Washington, such as we have made. We consecrate a great deal of nonsense because it was allowed by great men. There is none without his foible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist creating or seeking flawless heroes or geniuses. Recognize that admiration may blur faults; in art and character portrayals, keep realism about human foibles to avoid false deification. Great qualities often coexist with plain weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer universals (genius, magnetism) over momentary personal influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us go for universals; for the magnetism, not for the needles. Human life and its persons are poor empirical pretensions. A personal influence is an ignis fatuus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek the underlying, recurring principle or spirit in a work or person rather than being swayed by transient charisma or the momentary estimation of speakers. Judge by the universal quality that transcends ephemeral reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use particulars and anomalies as useful criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Anomalous facts... are of ideal use. They are good indications. Homoeopathy is insignificant as an art of healing, but of great value as criticism on the hygeia or medical practice of the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat deviations, peculiar theories, and oddities not merely as mistakes but as diagnostics that reveal limitations or blind spots in prevailing systems. In criticism or creative work, anomalous details can point to deeper truths and spur reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance the particular and the universal (rotate attention)
rubrics_metrics.description: We are amphibious creatures... having two sets of faculties, the particular and the catholic... We value total powers and effects, as the impression, the quality, the spirit of men and things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A creator should attend both to precise, localized detail (the particular) and to the larger, unifying vision (the universal). Nature distributes attention so that points come in succession to the meridian; likewise a work should let aspects appear in turn to form a new whole. Do not live only in abstractions, nor only in surface particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrate distributed, specialized genius and practical craft
rubrics_metrics.description: She loves better a wheelwright who dreams all night of wheels, and a groom who is part of his horse; for she is full of work, and these are her hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and value specialized, practical mastery rather than expecting every individual to be a universal genius. In creative communities, honor varied talents and the craftsmanship that sustains culture and art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate private character rather than over-relying on institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The antidote to this abuse of formal Government is the influence of private character, the growth of the Individual... To educate the wise man the State exists, and with the appearance of the wise man the State expires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For social and moral improvement, focus on forming individual character and conscience rather than primarily creating new laws or institutions. The mature individual (the 'wise man') embodies moral authority and reduces dependence on coercive structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and engage with works to find the universal, not merely the author
rubrics_metrics.description: I find the most pleasure in reading a book in a manner least flattering to the author... I read Proclus, and sometimes Plato, as I might read a dictionary, for a mechanical help to the fancy and the imagination... It is a greater joy to see the author's author, than himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying literature or sources, seek the enduring, universal contributions (the 'author's author' or the genius in the work) rather than idolizing the personal fame of the writer. Use texts to inform imagination and to extract lasting luminescence ('lustres') for your own work.
